overview: The Purépecha state centered its later capital at Tzintzuntzan in the Lake Pátzcuaro basin. Its political history is one part of a continuing Purépecha cultural tradition.

items.text: Tzintzuntzan concentrated political, economic and religious authority in the lake basin.
A pier linked Tzintzuntzan with other lake communities. Its hillside position provided broad visibility across the basin.
Craftworkers made objects in turquoise, obsidian, metal and clay, drawing on several technical traditions.
INAH distinguishes earlier El Opeño, Chupícuaro and Tingambato cultures from the later Purépecha state. These are regional archaeological phases, not successive names for one kingdom.
Purépecha cultural identity persisted beyond the precolonial state. A state's political transformation must not be displayed as the disappearance of its people.
Fishing was a major activity around Lake Pátzcuaro, connecting the capital's economy with lake resources.
Five temple platforms stood on Tzintzuntzan's main terrace, supporting wooden temples with thatched roofs.

sources.title: INAH: Tzintzuntzan, the Rise of the Purepecha State
